extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, trial judges, appellate counsel, and patent litigators advising trial strategy
extracted.subtask_description: Standards for admitting expert testimony in patent trials (qualification, relevance, reliability) and legal criteria for obviousness/JMOL review (KSR framework, motivation to combine, secondary considerations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Rule of Evidence 702 admissibility test
rubrics_metrics.description: If scientific, technical, or other specialized knowledge will assist the trier of fact to understand the evidence or to determine a fact in issue, a witness qualified as an expert by knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education may testify thereto in the form of an opinion or otherwise, if (1) the testimony is based upon sufficient facts or data, (2) the testimony is the product of reliable principles and methods, and (3) the witness has applied the principles and methods reliably to the facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court acts in a gatekeeping role under Daubert v. Merrell Dow and Kumho Tire; admissibility requires both relevance and reliability. Apply the three-prong Rule 702 inquiry to expert testimony in patent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification in the pertinent art required for technical issues
rubrics_metrics.description: A witness must be qualified as an expert by knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education in the pertinent art to testify on technical issues such as infringement or validity, which are analyzed from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent lawyers without relevant technical experience are not qualified to testify as technical experts on infringement, anticipation, obviousness, or underlying technical questions; such testimony may be excluded. A witness possessing ordinary skill in the art can be qualified—no requirement of 'more than ordinary skill.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible scope of patent-law-expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent-law experts may appropriately testify about general USPTO practice and procedure and related procedural matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts have allowed testimony directed to general patent office procedures (e.g., prosecution, reexamination). However, testimony should be confined to areas where the witness has demonstrated relevant expertise; many courts limit patent-law-expert testimony to practice/procedure rather than technical issues or legal conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on technical-opinion testimony absent pertinent-art expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: A witness not qualified in the pertinent art may not testify as an expert as to anticipation, the nature of the claimed invention, what a prior art reference discloses, whether asserted claims read on the prior art reference, or obviousness (including motivation to combine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Underlying factual questions (scope/content of prior art, differences between claimed invention and prior art, motivation to combine references) require technical expertise and are improper subjects for a patent-law expert lacking such expertise. Admission of such testimony 'serves only to cause mischief and confuse the factfinder.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on experts opining on legal conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts should not be permitted to instruct the jury on the applicable law or to give opinions on ultimate legal issues (e.g., the court's role in claim construction and ultimate legal determinations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony designed to instruct the jury on the law or to usurp the court’s role in legal conclusions is inadmissible. Courts have repeatedly cautioned against patent lawyers testifying as to proper claim interpretation or ultimate questions of infringement/validity without proper technical qualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for admission of expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Admission of expert testimony is within the discretion of the trial court and reviewed on appeal for abuse of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Acoustical Design, Seattle Box, Kumho Tire: appellate courts apply abuse-of-discretion standard when reviewing district court evidentiary rulings under Rule 702.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent claims are construed and questions such as what a prior art reference discloses or whether a claim would have been obvious are determined from the perspective of one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must evaluate disclosures, claim scope, and obviousness through the POSITA lens. A witness who is actually of ordinary skill in the art may be qualified to explain technical matters to the factfinder.

rubrics_metrics.name: JMOL standard on appeal (Sixth Circuit standard applied de novo)
rubrics_metrics.description: JMOL is appropriate when, viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the non-moving party (giving that party all reasonable inferences), there is no genuine issue of material fact for the jury and reasonable minds could come to but one conclusion in favor of the moving party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate review of a district court's JMOL uses the same standard as the district court; apply de novo review in this Circuit when evaluating the propriety of JMOL.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR obviousness framework for combining prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining known elements according to their established functions can be obvious where it 'simply arranges old elements with each performing the same function it had been known to perform' and yields no more than one would expect from such an arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person of ordinary skill may 'fit the teachings of multiple patents together like pieces of a puzzle.' If each element performs the same function in combination as it did separately and the result is predictable, the combination favors obviousness (KSR v. Teleflex).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigid teaching-suggestion-motivation (TSM) test not required
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should not rigidly apply the teaching, suggestion, or motivation test; lack of an explicit suggestion in the art to combine references does not preclude a finding of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation to combine may be found from the record and common sense reasoning of a POSITA; district court reliance on an absence of explicit suggestion can be erroneous, particularly post-KSR.

rubrics_metrics.name: When obviousness may be resolved as a matter of law
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the content of the prior art, the scope of the patent claim, and the level of ordinary skill in the art are not in material dispute, and the obviousness of the claim is apparent in light of these factors, summary judgment (or JMOL) is appropriate because the ultimate judgment is a legal determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If underlying factual inquiries are undisputed and the combination would have been obvious to a POSITA, courts may decide obviousness as a matter of law rather than leave it to the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight and role of secondary considerations (objective indicia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary considerations—such as long-felt but unresolved need, copying, commercial success, and praise—are relevant objective evidence of nonobviousness but cannot overcome a strong prima facie case of obviousness as a matter of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts should consider secondary considerations, but they are insufficient to save claims when the primary considerations show the claimed invention is obvious (cite Anderson's-Black Rock, Leapfrog, Agrizap, Dystar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation that is the 'work of the skillful mechanic' is not inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying known techniques to improve or adapt prior art in an expected way is the work of a skillful mechanic, not of an inventor, and thus may render a claim obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If incorporation of a known feature from one reference into another involves only routine work by a designer of ordinary skill, that supports a finding of obviousness (Hotchkiss / Sakraida reasoning).
